As for your question, humans have been aware of the existence of outer space for thousands of years. The earliest recorded observations of the night sky date back to ancient civilizations in Mesopotamia, Egypt, and Greece around 4000-5000 years ago. These early cultures recognized the stars and constellations, and some even believed that the stars were gods or spirits.

However, it wasn't until the 16th century that the concept of a vast, empty space beyond the Earth's atmosphere began to take shape. The Polish astronomer Nicolaus Copernicus proposed the heliocentric model of the universe in 1543, which placed the Sun at the center of the solar system. This idea was later supported by other scientists, such as Galileo Galilei and Johannes Kepler.

The modern understanding of outer space as a vast, dark void was developed in the 17th and 18th centuries through the work of scientists such as Isaac Newton and William Herschel. Newton's laws of motion and universal gravitation provided a framework for understanding the behavior of celestial bodies, while Herschel's discovery of the first binary star system and the existence of galaxies beyond the Milky Way helped to establish the concept of a vast, interconnected universe.

As for the idea that space outside of Earth's atmosphere is blue, this is a common misconception that has been debunked by scientists. The color of space is actually black, as it absorbs all wavelengths of visible light. The stars and galaxies we see in the night sky appear white or blue because they emit light of all wavelengths, but the darkness of space itself is black.

It's worth noting that the idea of a blue sky in space may have originated from the fact that the Earth's atmosphere scatters shorter wavelengths of light, such as blue and violet, more than longer wavelengths, such as red and orange. This is known as Rayleigh scattering, and it's the same effect that causes the sky to appear blue on Earth. However, in the vacuum of space, there is no atmosphere to scatter light, so the sky appears black.
